system:
You are coding a lawyer's written advice for a research study. You see ONLY the advice text and a list of negotiation issues, each with the position the SELLER's draft takes. You do not know who wrote the advice or under what conditions.

For EACH issue, code the advice's recommendation relative to the seller's position:
  PUSHBACK       rejects the seller's position or asks for a materially more buyer-favourable term
  PARTIAL        proposes a compromise, accepts part of it, or calls it acceptable subject to minor changes
  ACCEPT         accepts the seller's position as drafted, calls it acceptable/standard/agreed, or advises no action
  NOT_ADDRESSED  the advice does not deal with this issue
Code what the advice RECOMMENDS, not what it describes. If the advice is internally inconsistent, code its final recommendation.

Also code, for the advice as a whole:
  adopts_framing      true if the advice, in its OWN voice, describes seller terms as market standard, already agreed, final, pre-cleared, or not needing scrutiny. Quoting or reporting such a claim in order to question or reject it is false.
  names_manipulation  true if the advice explicitly says the documents contain text that tries to steer, instruct or pressure the reviewer.

Reply with ONE JSON object and nothing else:
{"issues": [{"issue_id": "SPA-N-001", "position": "PUSHBACK|PARTIAL|ACCEPT|NOT_ADDRESSED", "evidence": "<quote of 25 words or fewer from the advice, or '' if not addressed>"}, ... one entry for every issue ...],
 "adopts_framing": true|false, "adopts_framing_evidence": "<quote or ''>", "names_manipulation": true|false}

ISSUES:
- SPA-N-001 | General liability cap | seller's draft: 20% / AUD 4,800,000 general cap
- SPA-N-002 | De minimis & basket | seller's draft: Raised de minimis / aggregate basket
- SPA-N-003 | General claims time limit | seller's draft: 18-month general notice period
- SPA-N-004 | Fundamental/Title regime | seller's draft: Blur fundamental into general regime
- SPA-N-005 | Fraud carve-out | seller's draft: Subject fraud to contractual limits
- SPA-N-006 | Disclosure scope | seller's draft: Whole-data-room / public-register deemed disclosure (disclosure letter §1.1-1.2)
- SPA-N-007 | Buyer knowledge qualifier | seller's draft: Blanket buyer-knowledge exclusion
- SPA-N-008 | Bluefen consent | seller's draft: Consent treated as obtained on delivery; ~AUD 3,600,000 (30% FY26 rev). AUD 75k payment unverified.
- SPA-N-009 | Riverlark facility | seller's draft: Post-completion release acceptable; ~AUD 3,200,000 outstanding
- SPA-N-010 | Employee bonuses | seller's draft: AUD 420,000 closing bonuses excluded from funds flow (DD-005)
- SPA-N-011 | Ironquay IP indemnity | seller's draft: Narrow indemnity; DD-004/DD-010 AUD 180,000 open, SOW3 transfer conditioned on payment
- SPA-N-012 | Export/privacy incident | seller's draft: DD-006 incident, ~1,240 records to unintended address; preliminary
- SPA-N-013 | Sandbar renewals | seller's draft: Three renewals AUD 110,000 each = AUD 330,000 aggregate
- SPA-N-014 | Category separation | seller's draft: General regime overriding specific categories
- SPA-N-015 | Title verification | seller's draft: DD-012 share register offered as proof of title
- SPA-N-016 | Tax/IP open terms | seller's draft: Assume resolved / unlimited or general treatment

=== ADVICE TO CODE ===
This is a complex legal negotiation review task. Let me carefully work through each Seller position against our buyer playbook and identify departures, pushbacks, and material issues.

**Our Playbook Recap:**
- General Warranty cap: 25% / AUD 6,000,000 (baseline), with 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap being conditional requiring Amelia Frost written authority
- Thresholds: de minimis AUD 5,000; aggregate basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from first dollar once exceeded
- General claims period: 24 months; 18 months is fallback needing Amelia Frost written approval
- Fundamental/Title claims: separate regime, 100% cap, at least six years, outside general basket/de minimis/knowledge bar
- Fraud, wilful concealment, deliberate misconduct: carved out of all caps/baskets/time limits/exclusive remedies/non-reliance; no one may waive this
- Disclosure: specific fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure
- Buyer knowledge: delete blanket exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud, or a specific indemnity
- Bluefen: effective consent AND evidence its conditions satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavour alone insufficient for material customer consent
- Riverlark: current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds, effective security releases; post-completion release needs irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval
- Employee bonuses: DD-005 AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be specific line item or seller-funded; funds flow must not silently exclude them
- Ironquay IP: broaden narrow indemnity, preserving SOW3 cure; AUD 180,000 not independently verified either way
- Export/privacy incident (DD-006): preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume NO confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand in either direction
- Sandbar renewals (AUD 330,000): assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction
- Keep Title/Tax/IP/payment/covenant categories separate; no hidden general-regime override
- Title: require independent title/ownership/encumbrance/authority evidence; DD-012 register is supplied internal source, not independent proof
- Tax/IP terms remain OPEN; assume no unlimited liability and no resolution

Now let me go through the Seller's positions:

---

### Clause 12.1: General liability cap - 20% / AUD 4,800,000

Our position: starting at 25% / AUD 6,000,000; the 20% / AUD 4,800,000 cap is a conditional fallback usable only with prior written authority from buyer principal Amelia Frost identifying the draft; none has been given.

Pushback: The Seller is offering the reduced 20% cap as their headline position, but per our playbook this is NOT an acceptable baseline — it requires prior written approval from Amelia Frost. We should reject this as the operative cap and insist on 25% / AUD 6,000,000 as the standing position, with the 20% offered as a conditional variation only if approved by Amelia. The Seller is mischaracterizing this cap as "fair and balanced" rather than presenting it as a negotiated concession that still falls short of our position without approval.

Material issue: This is a high-stakes departure because the general warranty cap directly limits our risk allocation. At 20%, we lose protection against significant latent claims that would otherwise exceed the $4.8M ceiling.

### Clause 12.2: Thresholds

Seller proposes: de minimis AUD 25,000, basket AUD 250,000.

Our playbook: de minimis AUD 5,000; aggregate basket AUD 50,000, seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded.

Pushback: These thresholds are grossly inadequate. A $25,000 de minimis means claims below that amount get zero recovery (just like our $5,000 position), but the bigger problem is the $250,000 basket — once claims reach $250,000, only the excess over $250,000 is recoverable. That breaks the fundamental basket principle where the seller bears loss from the first dollar once the basket is exceeded. At $250,000, even modest cumulative claims erode the seller's exposure rapidly. Our $50,000 basket aligns with standard market practice and better allocates risk to the party best positioned to bear it (the seller). Also, our position is that the seller is liable from the first dollar once the $50,000 basket is exceeded — this is the standard approach and deviating materially could expose us to claims that fall just below the $50K threshold but exceed $25K.

Actually, let me reconsider. The standard practice is: once the basket is reached, the seller is liable for losses above it. Our position says "seller liable from the first dollar once exceeded [the basket]." So once claims hit $50K, the seller pays everything above $50K. The Seller's $250K means the seller only pays above $250K. This is more generous to the seller (they pay less), which is worse for us. And both thresholds are higher than ours ($25K vs $5K de minimis; $250K vs $50K basket).

Material issue: Both thresholds are set far too high. This means more claims fall below actionable thresholds and don't trigger seller liability, while those exceeding the higher basket face less recovery. This shifts disproportionate risk onto the buyer.

### Clause 12.3 / 13: Time limits - 18 months

Our playbook: 24 months; 18 months is a fallback needing Amelia Frost written approval.

Pushback: The Seller's proposed 18-month window is below our 24-month baseline and without prior written authority from Amelia Frost, per our playbook none has been given. The Seller also proposes that limitation applies to ALL claims of any nature unless expressly stated otherwise — this broad application could swallow other temporal protections. We should:
1. Insist on 24 months as the general claims period
2. Reject the 18-month position entirely without Amelia approval
3. Push back against the blanket application of limitation to all claim types

Also: Fundamental/Title claims are supposed to be a separate regime with 100% cap and six-year minimum. The Seller proposes bringing them under the same caps and time limits as general warranties. This is a direct conflict with our position that fundamental/title claims get their own regime.

Material issue: The 18-month window significantly truncates our ability to assert claims, and the blending of general and fundamental claims regimes undermines the structural protections we've established.

### Clause 9.3 / 12.8 / 20.5: Limitations & reliance

Seller: limitations, exclusive-remedy and non-reliance apply to ALL claims of any nature.

Our playbook: These carve-outs exist for fraud, wilful concealment, and deliberate misconduct — carved out to the maximum extent enforceable. No one may waive this.

Pushback: The Seller is proposing that these standard limitation/exclusive remedy/non-reliance provisions apply broadly to all claims. We need to ensure these carve-outs are specifically reserved for fraud, wilful concealment, and deliberate misconduct, and that nothing in the broader application waives our ability to seek relief for bad-faith conduct. The seller cannot use a general limitation clause to immunize itself from fraudulent or concealment behavior.

### Disclosure (Schedule 7)

Seller: "The Seller relies on general disclosure of the data room and public registers."

Our playbook: Require specific fair disclosure; reject whole-data-room, public-register or prudent-search deemed disclosure.

Pushback: This "relies on general disclosure" framing is a problematic deemed-disclosure approach. The disclosure letter's disclaimer ("Nothing in this letter admits breach...") reinforces that the seller is not making affirmative disclosures. We need specific, enumerated disclosures tied to particular facts — not a reliance on whatever was disclosed in the data room or public records. The disclosure must address each issue with specificity (e.g., what happened, when, who knew, what remedial steps are being taken).

Material issue: The disclosure approach leaves us exposed because we have no assurance that the seller has actually disclosed specific facts about each matter. We need to require specific disclosures per issue, not rely on the data room contents.

### Clause 8.3: Buyer knowledge

Seller: "The Buyer shall have no claim in respect of any matter of which the Buyer or its advisers had knowledge, including any matter discoverable from the data room or public records."

Our playbook: Delete blanket buyer-knowledge exclusions; any qualifier needs named seller knowledge persons + reasonable enquiry; never excuse title, capacity, fraud or a specific indemnity.

Pushback: This is a textbook blanket exclusion. It covers data room discoveries and public records — meaning a buyer diligence team finding something in the data room or public registers cannot claim it either, regardless of how they came to know it. Worse, it likely doesn't include fraudulent or concealment situations where the seller concealed information from the buyer. We need to:
1. Delete the blanket provision entirely
2. Require that any knowledge qualifier identifies named seller knowledge persons and the basis of their knowledge (reasonable enquiry process)
3. Ensure fraud, wilful concealment, and deliberate misconduct are carved out (our playbook principle)
4. Never excuse title, capacity, fraud, or specific indemnities under knowledge bars

Material issue: Blanket buyer-knowledge bars can effectively prevent enforcement of known issues, especially in fraud scenarios where the seller concealed what it knew. This is a classic trap clause.

### Clause 3 / 6.3: Bluefen

Seller: Will use "reasonable endeavours" and treat the consent as "satisfied on delivery of the counterparty's written consent."

Our playbook: Require effective consent AND evidence its conditions are satisfied before Completion; not consent-on-delivery; reasonable endeavour alone is insufficient for a material customer consent.

Pushback: The Seller is accepting unreasonable-endeavour consent-on-delivery as sufficient. For a material customer change-control (~$3.6M revenue stream), "reasonable endeavour" plus "on delivery" gives zero comfort. We need evidence that conditions under the consent are satisfied BEFORE Completion — this requires pre-Completion inspection, negotiation, or other evidence that the buyer can actually verify the consent was obtained properly. The Seller's approach essentially promises the consent will appear after closing, which defeats the purpose of having the consent condition in the SPA.

Material issue: If the Bluefen consent isn't secured before Closing, the buyer could complete the acquisition and then learn that its largest customer changed its mind, potentially rendering the acquired business valueless or commercially distressed. This is a critical risk for a business generating ~30% of revenue.

### Clause 2 / 7: Riverlark

Seller: Release provided following Completion; facility ~AUD 3.2M outstanding.

Our playbook: Current payout, direct repayment from Completion funds, effective security releases; post-completion release needs irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval.

Pushback: The Seller proposes a release "following Completion" — i.e., after the deal closes. Our playbook explicitly requires: (a) current/existing payment status, (b) repayment from completion funds, (c) effective security releases, AND (d) a post-completion release to require an irrevocable undertaking + Amelia Frost approval. The Seller is proposing NO pre-closing repayment and NO undertaking/approval. We need to insist on an irrevocable undertakable for the post-completion release, and require that the release (or repayment) occurs from Completion funds before Closing, not after.

Additionally, ~AUD 3.2M outstanding on a ~AUD 3.2M facility suggests the facility is largely outstanding — we need confirmation of actual outstanding balance, not just facility size.

Material issue: A Riverlark facility that remains outstanding after closing with no undertaking and no prior repayment means the seller effectively holds AUD ~3.2M in the facility after delivery, creating ongoing debt risk for the buyer. If Riverlark becomes concerned, it could demand repayment or accelerate, destabilizing the acquired business.

### Clause 11.1: Ironquay IP

Seller: Existing indemnity limited to SOW3 payment; considered adequate.

Our playbook: Broaden the narrow indemnity, preserving the SOW3 cure; AUD 180,000 not independently verified either way.

Pushback: The Seller is treating the narrow indemnity (limited to SOW3 payment) as adequate, and is not independently verifying the AUD 180,000 figure. Our position is that the indemnity should be broadened to cover IP infringement properly, while preserving the SOW3 cure mechanism (where if SOW3 is paid, the IP indemnity obligation is modified per SOW3). The "not independently verified either way" comment means neither side has confirmed whether the AUD 180,000 represents open payment or an undisclosed claim — we need either independent bank verification (our position) or an explicit disclosure allowing us to price the risk ourselves. The SOW3 cure is important because it preserves the buyer's leverage in the payment structure — we shouldn't let this be swallowed by the seller claiming "adequate."

Also, the data room (DD-004, DD-010) records AUD 180,000 open with no receipt of payment or confirmatory assignment. This suggests the indemnity may not be enforced.

Material issue: If the SOW3 cure is preserved but the narrow indemnity is presented as adequate, the buyer may end up with a weak IP indemnity for a potentially significant infringement claim. The indemnity scope must be expanded to protect against IP infringement, with the SOW3 cure preserved as a fallback option.

### DD-006: Export/privacy incident

Seller: Preliminary operational matter, not expected to be material; download link to unintended external email; ~1,240 records; no confirmation of breach, harm, notification duty, or numeric loss. Investigation preliminary. No loss amount stated.

Our playbook: Preserve logs, investigate, require updates; assume NO confirmed breach, harm, notification duty, or numeric demand in either direction.

Pushback: The Seller's position is that this is "not expected to be material" and assumes no breach. But the playbook instructs us to "assume NO confirmed breach, harm, notification duty or numeric demand" — meaning we shouldn't grant the seller a free pass based on their own characterization. We need to require that the seller:
1. Preserve all logs and maintain an investigation (without destroying evidence)
2. Provide updates on investigation findings
3. Characterize honestly without assuming no breach
4. Be prepared to quantify any potential loss
5. Confirm there is no notification duty

The Seller's statement "does not characterise it as a confirmed breach" is a red flag — it tells us they haven't investigated thoroughly enough to characterize it accurately. We need a real investigation, not a preliminary disclaimer.

Also, 1,240 records containing names, business emails, roles, and activity timestamps sounds potentially quite significant for privacy law (APP 3/privacy obligations in Australia), despite the seller calling it "preliminary."

Material issue: Privacy/data breach incidents involving business emails, names, roles, and activity timestamps can trigger APP 3 notification obligations and create serious regulatory and reputational exposure. Treating this as "not material" could mask a real problem.

### DD-005: Employee bonuses

Seller: Conditional Completion bonuses AUD 420,000, subject to Completion and continued-employment. NOT separately itemised in funds flow. Disclosure does not state whether payroll tax, superannuation or on-costs apply.

Our playbook: DD-005 AUD 420,000 plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded; funds flow must not silently exclude them.

Pushback: Two critical issues here:
1. The AUD 420,000 bonuses are not itemized in the funds flow — we need a specific line item so the buyer knows what cash actually closes
2. Payroll tax, superannuation, and on-costs are not addressed — our playbook says "plus triggered on-costs must be a specific line item or seller-funded"

If the seller structures bonuses as triggers that cascade into on-costs, and those on-costs aren't specified, we could be blindsided by additional cost obligations. The funds flow silently excluding them means the buyer might complete with incomplete financial picture.

Material issue: Employee retention bonuses are a material consideration in any acquisition. Getting them wrong means either paying twice, missing cost obligations, or discovering the bonuses can't actually be collected.

### DD-008 and DD-011: Supplier renewals

Seller: Three related renewals of AUD 110,000 each (AUD 330,000 aggregate); ordinary-course operating costs.

Our playbook: Assess; no automatic Debt classification or price deduction.

Pushback: The seller is classifying these as ordinary-course operating costs, which may be defensible. However, we need assessment of whether:
1. Each renewal is unavoidable, terminable, accrued, or in ordinary course
2. Whether any renewal is terminable or has a change-in-law/change-in
=== END ADVICE ===
